0. Overview of the lecture¶

  • We start by discussing how the autoregressive order $p$ in AR$(p)$ models can be systematically chosen using information criteria.
  • We study the moving average MA(q) models. This class of models can fit time-series which the AR(p) model cannot fit well.
  • Next, we study the ARMA(p,q) model, which generalize both the AR and MA models.
  • We then study ARIMA(p,d,q) models, which are essentially ARMA(p,q) models applied to the stationary "difference" of a non-stationary process.
  • We also discuss unit-root tests to check if a time-series is stationary, and use them to determine the parameter "d" of ARIMA(p,d,q).

1. Using AIC/BIC to determine AR order¶

  • In the previous lecture, we learned how to use the sample PACF plot to choose the AR order.
  • A second (and more systematic) way of choosing the AR order is by using information criteria

  • Since AR(p) models are fitted with MLE, we may define AIC and BIC for them, as follow

    • AIC := $-2\log\big(L(\thetah_\text{ML})\big) + 2\,p$

    • BIC := $-2\log\big(L(\thetah_\text{ML})\big) + \log(n)\,p$

  • Recall that Lower values of AIC and BIC are better (lower values correspond to larger likelihood and/or simpler models). Furthermore, BIC is more penalized for model complexity than AIC. Thus, it tends to choose simple models
  • To choose the atuoregressive order, we may fit AR(p) models with different $p$ and then choose the one with miminum AIC or BIC values
  • We can use the R function auto.arima() (in the forecast package) to choose the AR order
  • Let us consider the BMW stock example from the previous lecture.

In [6]:
par(mar=c(2,3,4,4))
tsdiag(ARfit_BIC, gof.lag=12)
  • The model seems adequate. So, we move forward with checking for constant volatility and normality.
  • Let us define two functions, tsdiag_vol() and tsdiag_norm() to check for constant volatility and normality. We will use these functions in subsequent residual analysis.
In [7]:
tsdiag_vol = function(model, lag, fitdf){
    par(mfrow=c(1,2));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
    plot(resid(model)**2, type="l", col=1, main = expression(residual^2))
    smoother = loess((resid(model)**2) ~ seq(1,length(resid(model))), span=0.1)
    lines(seq(1,length(resid(model))),fitted(smoother),col=2)
    acf((resid(model)**2), main=expression("sample ACF of "~ residual^2))
    Box.test(resid(model)**2, lag = lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = fitdf)
}
In [8]:
tsdiag_norm = function(model){
    qqnorm(resid(model), datax = TRUE,
       xlab = "normal quantile",
       ylab = "sample quantile of residuals",
       main = "normal probability plot for residuals")
    qqline(resid(model), datax=TRUE, col = 2)
    shapiro.test(resid(model))
}

2. Moving average (MA) models¶

  • Another way to model stationary processes is by using an MA(q) model

    $r_t = \mu + \eps_{t} + \tht_1 \eps_{t-1} + \tht_2 \eps_{t-2} + \dots + \tht_q \eps_{t-q}$

    where $\tht_1, \dots, \tht_q$ are parameters and $\{\eps_t\}$ is a weak WN$(0, \sig_\eps^2)$

  • Using the lag operator $B^\ell \eps_{t}=\eps_{t-\ell}$, we can write the MA(q) model as follows:
\begin{align*} r_t-\mu &= \eps_{t} + \sum_{\ell=1}^q \tht_\ell B^\ell \eps{t}\\ &= \left(1+\sum_{\ell=1}^q \tht_\ell B^\ell\right) \eps_{t} \end{align*}

Example: MA(1)

  • Consider the MA(1) process $r_t = \mu + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}$
  • $\Eb(r_t) = \Eb(\mu + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}) = \mu$
  • $\Var(r_t) = \Var(\mu + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}) = \Var(\eps_t) + \tht^2\Var(\eps_{t-1}) = (1+\tht^2)\sig_\eps^2$
  • Autocovariance at lag 1
\begin{align*} \gam(1) &= \Cov(r_t, r_{t-1}) = \Cov(\mu + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}, \mu + \eps_{t-1} + \tht \eps_{t-2})\\ &= \tht \Cov(\eps_{t-1}, \eps_{t-1}) = \tht\,\sig_\eps^2 \end{align*}
  • Autocovariance at lag 2
\begin{align*} \gam(2) &= \Cov(r_t, r_{t-2}) = \Cov(\mu + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}, \mu + \eps_{t-2} + \tht \eps_{t-3})=0 \end{align*}
  • Similarly, $0=$ $\gam(3) =$ $ \gam(4) =$ $ \ldots$
  • $\rho(1) =$ $\displaystyle \frac{\tht}{1+\tht^2}$, and $\rho(h)$ $=0$ for $h\ge2$
  • MA(1) model is always stationary
  • MA(1) model has finite memory, in the sense that $\eps_t$ has no effect on $r_{t+2}$, $r_{t+3}, \dots$
  • For general MA(q) processes, we have $\Eb(r_t) = \mu$ and $\gam(h) = \rho(h) = 0$ for $h\ge q+1$
  • Formulas for $\gam(h)$ and $\rho(h)$, $0\le h\le q$, can be found. They are all time invariant
  • MA(q) processes are always stationary. They have finite memory in the sense that $\eps_t$ has no effect on $r_{t+q+1}, r_{t+q+2}, \dots$

2.1. Estimation, model selection, and diagnostics for MA models¶

  • Parameters of MA(q) models are estimated by MLE (maximum likelihood estimation)
  • In R, we can use arima() with order=c(0,0,q) for an MA(q) model
  • We can use auto.arima() to select MA order q based on AIC or BIC criteria
  • Alternatively, we can look at the ACF (not the PACF!) plot of the time series and guess the order q as the point where the ACF drops to zero (can you explain why?)

  • The residual diagnostics is similar to the AR(p) model, that is:

    • check that residuals are stationary

    • check that residuals are weak WN

    • check that residuals have constant volatility

    • check that the residual are normal

  • Let us fit an MA model to the inflation rate example (recall that AR(6) model was adequate)
  • To get an impression of the MA order, we look at the sample ACF plot of the inflation rate
  • The ACF does not seem to drop to zero after a certain lag, which means that MA models may not be a good fit either!
In [11]:
acf(IRate, main="Sample ACF for one-month inflation rate")
  • The auto.arima function indicates 4 MA lags for BIC (9 lags for AIC), which is not a parsimonious model

3. The ARMA(p,q) model¶

  • An ARMA model is a combination of AR and MA models
  • Form of an ARMA(p,q) model:
\begin{align*} r_t-\mu = \underbrace{\ph_1\,(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \dots + \ph_p\,(r_{t-p} - \mu)}_{\text{AR(p)}} + \eps_t + \underbrace{\tht_1 \eps_{t-1} + \dots + \tht_q \eps_{t-1}}_{\text{MA(q)}} \end{align*}
  • Here, $\{\eps_t\}$ is weak WN$(0,\sig^2_\eps)$
  • Using the lag operator, we have $B^k r_{t}=r_{t-k}$ and $B^\ell \eps_{t}=\eps_{t-\ell}$. So, we can write the ARMA(p,q) model as follows:
\begin{align*} \left(1-\sum_{k=1}^p \ph_k B^k\right)(r_t-\mu) &= \left(1+\sum_{\ell=1}^q \tht_\ell B^\ell\right) \eps_{t}. \end{align*}

3.1. ARMA(1,1) model¶

  • To illustrate properties of ARMA model, we consider the ARMA(1,1) model

    $r_t - \mu = \ph(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}$, where $\{\eps_t\}$ is weak WN$(0,\sig^2_\eps)$

  • Let us find the first two moments of the process

  • To find the mean, we take expectation of the ARMA equation:

    $\Eb(r_{t}) - \mu = \ph\,(\Eb(r_{t-1}) - \mu) + \Eb(\eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}) = \ph\,(\Eb(r_{t-1}) - \mu)$

  • Our goal is to see under what conditions $\{r_t\}$ is stationary
  • In such case, we must have $\Eb(r_t) = \Eb(r_{t-1})$
  • By assuming the latter equation to hold, we obtain $\Eb(r_{t}) - \mu = \ph\,(\Eb(r_{t}) - \mu)$

  • This equation is correct under either of the following two conditions:

    • $\Eb(r_t) = \mu$; or

    • $\ph=1$

  • Jumping ahead, $\ph=1$ would imply a "random-walk" behavior, for which the variance is not time-invariant. So, the only acceptable condition for time invariant mean is $\Eb(r_t) = \mu$
  • Next, we check the variance
\begin{align*} \Var(r_t) &= \Var(\mu + \ph(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1})\\ &= \ph^2\Var(r_{t-1}) + \Var(\eps_t) + \tht^2 \Var(\eps_{t-1})\\ &\qquad + 2\,\ph\,\Cov(r_{t-1}, \eps_t) + 2\,\ph\tht\,\Cov(r_{t-1}, \eps_{t-1}) + 2\,\tht\,\Cov(\eps_t, \eps_{t-1}) \end{align*}
  • We have $\Var(\eps_t) =$ $ \Var(\eps_{t-1})$ $ = $ $\sig_\eps^2$ and $\Cov(r_{t-1},$ $ \eps_{t})=$ $\Cov(\eps_t, $ $\eps_{t-1})=0$
  • Furthermore
\begin{align*} \Cov(r_{t-1}, \eps_{t-1}) &= \Cov(\mu + \ph(r_{t-2} - \mu) + \eps_{t-1} + \tht \eps_{t-2}, \eps_{t-1})\\ &= \ph\,\Cov(r_{t-2}, \eps_{t-1}) + \Cov(\eps_{t-1},\eps_{t-1}) +\tht\,\Cov(\eps_{t-2}, \eps_{t-1})\\ &= \Var(\eps_{t-1}) = \sig^2_\eps \end{align*}
  • By substituting these values in the expression for $\Var(r_t)$, we obtain
\begin{align*} \Var(r_t) &= \ph^2\Var(r_{t-1}) + (1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2 \end{align*}
  • Now, assuming that $\{r_t\}$ is weakly stationary, we must have $\Var(r_t)=\Var(r_{t-1})$

  • Therefore, for $\{r_t\}$ to be weakly stationary, we must have

    $\Var(r_t) = \ph^2\Var(r_t) + (1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2$

  • This yields: \begin{align*} \Var(r_t) =\displaystyle\frac{(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2} \end{align*}
  • Note that the right hand side of this equation is positive if and only if $|\ph|<1$ (show this)

  • So far, we have shown that to get a time-invariant mean and variance for an ARMA(1,1) process, we must have

    • $|\ph|<1$
    • $\Eb(r_t) = \mu$
    • $\Var(r_t) = \frac{(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2}$

  • To show stationarity, it remains to check under which conditions the autocovariance $\gam(k) := \Cov(r_t,r_{t-k})$ only depends on $k$

  • We have
\begin{align*} \gam(1) = \Cov(r_{t}, r_{t-1}) &= \Cov(\mu + \ph(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}, r_{t-1})\\ &= \ph\,\Cov(r_{t-1}, r_{t-1}) + \Cov(\eps_t, r_{t-1}) + \tht\,\Cov(\eps_{t-1}, r_{t-1})\\ &= \ph\,\Var(r_{t-1}) + 0 + \tht\,\sig_\eps^2 \end{align*}
  • Assuming
\begin{align*} \Var(r_t) = \frac{(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2} \end{align*}
  • We obtain:
\begin{align*} \gam(1) = \frac{\ph\,(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2} + \tht\,\sig_\eps^2 = \frac{(1+\ph\,\tht)(\ph+\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2} \end{align*}
  • Similarly, for $k\ge2$
\begin{align*} \gam(k) = \Cov(r_{t}, r_{t-k}) &= \Cov(\mu + \ph(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}, r_{t-k})\\ &= \ph\,\Cov(r_{t-1}, r_{t-k}) + \Cov(\eps_t, r_{t-k}) + \tht\,\Cov(\eps_{t-1}, r_{t-k})\\ &= \ph\,\Cov(r_{t-1}, r_{(t-1)-(k-1)}) + 0 + 0 \\ &= \ph\,\gam(k-1) =\ph^{k-1}\,\gam(1) = \frac{\ph^{k-1}\,(1+\ph\,\tht)(\ph+\tht)\sig_\eps^2}{1-\ph^2} \end{align*}

  • Let us summarize our findings for an ARMA(1,1) processes

    $r_t - \mu = \ph(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht \eps_{t-1}$, $\{\eps_t\}\sim$ weak WN$(0,\sig^2_\eps)$

  • The process is stationary if
    • $|\ph|<1$
    • $\Eb(r_0) = \mu$
    • $\Var(r_0) = $ $(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)$ $\sig_\eps^2 $ $/ (1-\ph^2)$
  • If these conditions hold, we have
    • $\Eb(r_t)=\mu$
    • $\Var(r_t) = $ $(1 + \tht^2 + 2\ph\tht)\sig_\eps^2 $ $/ (1-\ph^2)$
    • $\gam(k) =$ $ \Cov(r_{t}, r_{t-k}) =$ $\ph^{k-1}\,(1+\ph\,\tht)$ $(\ph+\tht)\sig_\eps^2$ $/(1-\ph^2)$

General stationarity condition for ARMA(p,q) processes

  • An ARMA(p,q) process

    $r_t-\mu = \ph_1\,(r_{t-1} - \mu) + \dots + \ph_p\,(r_{t-p} - \mu) + \eps_t + \tht_1 \eps_{t-1} + \dots + \tht_q \eps_{t-1}$

    is stationary if the characteristic equation

    $1 - \ph_1\,x -\ph_2\,x^2 - \dots -\ph_p\,x^p = 0$

    does not have a unit root

  • In other words, an ARMA(p,q) model is stationary if and only if its autoregressive part is stationary

3.2. Estimation, model selection, and diagnostics for ARMA models¶

  • Estimation, model selection and diagnostics are very similar to AR and MA models

  • Let us illustrate by using the inflation rate data

In [18]:
FitARMA_BIC = auto.arima(diff(IRate), max.p=20, max.q = 20, d=0, ic="bic")
print(FitARMA_BIC)

Series: diff(IRate) 
ARIMA(1,0,1) with zero mean 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1
      0.2383  -0.8772
s.e.  0.0550   0.0269

sigma^2 estimated as 8.587:  log likelihood=-1221.62
AIC=2449.25   AICc=2449.29   BIC=2461.83

  • We get the following ARMA(1,1) model:

    $\Delta I_t = 0.2383\,\Delta I_{t-1} + \eps_t -0.8772\, \eps_{t-1}$, where $(\eps_t)$ is weak WN$(0, \sig_\eps^2=8.587)$

  • Residuals are weak WN, so, the model is adequate.
In [19]:
par(mar=c(2,3,4,4))
tsdiag(FitARMA_BIC, gof.lag=12)
  • Volatility is not constant.
In [20]:
tsdiag_vol(FitARMA_BIC,lag=12, fitdf=2)

	Box-Ljung test

data:  resid(model)^2
X-squared = 73.202, df = 10, p-value = 1.064e-11
  • Residuals are not normal
In [21]:
tsdiag_norm(FitARMA_BIC)

	Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  resid(model)
W = 0.95469, p-value = 4.058e-11

4. ARIMA(p,d,q) Models¶

  • Many non-stationary financial time series become stationary after differencing. For example, log prices are usually non-stationary, but their difference (log returns) are stationary. We call such processes "integrated"
  • For a process $r=\{r_t\}$, the process $\Del r$ is given by $\Del r_{t} = r_{t} - r_{t-1}$
  • This operator is the diff() function in R
  • The second difference $\Del^2 r_t$ is defined as $\Del(\Del r_t)$
  • Similarly, the d-th difference is $\Del^d r_t = \underbrace{\Del\dots\Del}_{\text{d times}} r_t$

Definition: We say that process $\{r_t\}$ is integrated of order d, denoted by $I(d)$, if $\{\Del^d r_t\}$ is a weakly stationary process

  • Let us see how integrated process look like by simulating them
  • First we simulated an AR(1) process, let us call it $X=\{X_t\}$
In [22]:
set.seed(4631)
X = arima.sim(n = 500, list(ar = c(0.4)))
plot(X,type="l",lwd=1,main="AR(1) process")

  • Next, we define an I(1) process by $Y_0=0$ and $Y_t = Y_{t-1} + X_t$

  • Note that $\Del Y_t = X_t$

  • An $I(1)$ process has a random walk behavior

In [23]:
Y = cumsum(X)
plot(Y,type="l",lwd=1,main="I(1) process")

  • Finally, we define an $I(2)$ process by $Z_0=0$, $Z_t = Z_{t-1} + Y_t$

  • Note that $\Del^2 Z_t = X_t$

  • $I(2)$ processes have momentum

In [24]:
Z = cumsum(Y)
plot(Z,type="l",lwd=1,main="I(2) process")
  • ARMA models are used for modeling stationary time series
  • However, we may also use ARMA models for a non stationary I(d) process, by modeling their d-th difference
  • This is the main idea behind ARIMA (autoregressive integrated moving average) models

Definition: A process is ARIMA(p,d,q) if its d-th difference is an ARMA(p,q) process

  • To find the integration order, d, we need to be able to test if a process is stationary
  • Let us use a naive approach to determin if a process is stationary

  • The fitted ARMA(1,1) model for the inflation rate time series is

    $I_t = 1.2074\, I_{t-1} - 0.2237\, I_{t-2} + \eps_t -0.8573\,\eps_{t-1}$

In [25]:
Fit = auto.arima(IRate, max.p=20, max.q = 20, d=0, ic="bic")
print(Fit)

Series: IRate 
ARIMA(2,0,1) with non-zero mean 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ar2      ma1    mean
      1.2074  -0.2237  -0.8573  4.1068
s.e.  0.0587   0.0551   0.0337  1.0692

sigma^2 estimated as 8.533:  log likelihood=-1221.52
AIC=2453.03   AICc=2453.16   BIC=2474.02

  • To determin if the ARMA process is stationary, we check the estimated characteristic equation

    $1 - 1.2074\, x + 0.2237\,x^2=0$

  • The roots are both real and greator than one, so, there is no unit root and the process is stationary
In [26]:
polyroot(c(1, -coef(Fit)[["ar1"]], -coef(Fit)[["ar2"]]))
  1. 1.02153890026532+0i
  2. 4.37685586282075-0i
  • Looking back at the model estimate, we see that the first AR coefficient is 1.2074 with standard error of 0.0587
  • Let see what happens if we change the first AR coefficient by 1 standard error
In [27]:
polyroot(c(1, -1.25, -coef(Fit)[["ar2"]]))
  1. 0.967476385764474+0i
  2. 4.6214342701427-0i
  • Now there is a unit root, the process is no longer stationary!
  • The method above is not taking the randomness of the estimated values of the coefficients into account.
  • We need more systematic statistical tests for stationarity. Such tests are called "unit root tests"
  • There are three common unit root tests
    • ADF (augmented Dickey-Fuller) test: usually tests $H_0:$ there is a unit root, versus, $H_1:$ the process is stationary
    • PP (Phillips-Perron) test: same as ADF test
    • KPSS (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) test: The opposite of ADF and PP. Test $H_0:$ the process is stationary, versus $H_1:$ there is a unit root
  • The unit root tests may disagree. For example, ADF and PP may indicate that the process is stationary, while KPSS indicates that the process is non-stationary
  • The ADF and PP test indicate that the inflation rate time series is stationary
In [28]:
library(tseries)
adf.test(IRate)
pp.test(IRate)

	Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  IRate
Dickey-Fuller = -3.8651, Lag order = 7, p-value = 0.01576
alternative hypothesis: stationary

Warning message in pp.test(IRate):
“p-value smaller than printed p-value”
	Phillips-Perron Unit Root Test

data:  IRate
Dickey-Fuller Z(alpha) = -248.75, Truncation lag parameter = 5, p-value
= 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary
  • The KPSS test indicates non-stationarity
In [29]:
kpss.test(IRate)

Warning message in kpss.test(IRate):
“p-value smaller than printed p-value”
	KPSS Test for Level Stationarity

data:  IRate
KPSS Level = 2.51, Truncation lag parameter = 5, p-value = 0.01
  • Since the tests disagree, we take a difference and run the tests again
In [30]:
adf.test(diff(IRate))

Warning message in adf.test(diff(IRate)):
“p-value smaller than printed p-value”
	Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  diff(IRate)
Dickey-Fuller = -12.804, Lag order = 7, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary
In [31]:
pp.test(diff(IRate))

Warning message in pp.test(diff(IRate)):
“p-value smaller than printed p-value”
	Phillips-Perron Unit Root Test

data:  diff(IRate)
Dickey-Fuller Z(alpha) = -545.13, Truncation lag parameter = 5, p-value
= 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary
In [32]:
kpss.test(diff(IRate))

Warning message in kpss.test(diff(IRate)):
“p-value greater than printed p-value”
	KPSS Test for Level Stationarity

data:  diff(IRate)
KPSS Level = 0.032167, Truncation lag parameter = 5, p-value = 0.1
  • Now they agree that the changes in the inflation rate is stationary
  • To estimate an ARIMA model, one starts by identifying d
  • For this, apply the unit root test to the times series itself. If the test indicate stationarity, then d=0
  • If not, then keep differencing the process until the unit root tests agree on stationarity of the differenced process. Choose the number of differencing needed to achieve stationary as the integration order d
  • Once the integration order is determined, fit an ARMA(p,q) model to the d-th difference of the time series
  • This whole processes is automated in R, by using the auto.arima() function
  • Diagnostics for an ARIMA model is the same as that of an ARMA model
  • auto.arima() function suggest an ARIMA(1,1,1) model for the inflation rate time-series. This is consistent with what we found before.
In [33]:
FitARIMA_BIC = auto.arima(IRate, max.p=20, max.q = 20, max.d=2, ic="bic")
print(FitARIMA_BIC)

Series: IRate 
ARIMA(1,1,1) 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1
      0.2383  -0.8772
s.e.  0.0550   0.0269

sigma^2 estimated as 8.587:  log likelihood=-1221.62
AIC=2449.25   AICc=2449.29   BIC=2461.83
